title: The Forgotten God
subtitle: A five-session study on the Holy Spirit, the personal presence of God who gives life.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have spent years in church and somehow ended up with two persons of the Trinity they could describe and a third they could not. The Father they picture. The Son they love. The Spirit has been left a kind of holy vapor, a power source, an influence, the part of God you mention at the end of a prayer and then forget. This is not a small mistake. It is the loss of God himself, present, personal, indwelling, the very breath by which the dead are made alive. The study walks slowly through five movements. Who the Spirit is and why the church treats him as an afterthought. The new birth, regeneration, the Spirit who raises the spiritually dead, including the writer, who was an atheist until the Spirit did the one thing argument never could. The slow work of the fruit and the difference between being changed and merely performing. The contested question of the gifts, where continuationist and cessationist are both given their strongest case and the group is held together across the divide. And the Spirit in our weakness, the One who prays in us when we have no words, the down payment of a world being made new.

This is not a study that will pick the group's side in the old fights over tongues and prophecy and healing. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The continuationist case will be put at full strength and so will the cessationist, and the aim is a room that can disagree about gifts while worshiping the same Spirit. Most of all the study implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He spent years certain there was no God and no soul and no Spirit, and the thing that finally undid him was not a better argument. It was a presence he had no category for. He writes from inside the new birth he did not author and cannot explain. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Spirit We Ignore
sessions.aim: To recover the Holy Spirit as fully God and fully personal, not a force the church switches on for emotional moments and a power source it forgets the rest of the time, and to face honestly why we have made the third person of the Trinity an afterthought.
sessions.summary: Ask most Christians who the Holy Spirit is and you will get a long pause, then something about a feeling, a power, an influence. The Father and the Son they can describe. The Spirit they cannot, and that loss is not academic. Francis Chan called him the forgotten God, and he was right, because we have functionally reduced God himself to a vapor. The first question is not what the Spirit does. It is who the Spirit is. Bell takes the strong form of two errors that pull against each other. The first treats the Spirit as a force, an it, a divine electricity that fills you and makes you feel things, and there is a true instinct under it, that the Spirit really is power, really does fill, really is felt. The second overcorrects so hard against emotionalism that the Spirit becomes a footnote in a doctrine of God, true on paper and dead in practice, and there is a true instinct there too, a proper fear of making faith a search for feelings. Bell will not let either win. The Spirit is not a force, which refutes the first, because Scripture says he can be grieved, lied to, resisted, and only a person can be grieved. And the Spirit is not a footnote, which refutes the second, because he is the very presence of God now living inside the people of God. He is God, of one being with the Father and the Son. He is personal, he speaks and wills and loves. And he is here, not an influence sent from a distance but God himself indwelling. The reason we forget him is not that he is unimportant. It is that he is humble. He does not point to himself. He points to Christ. We mistook his self-effacement for absence.

keyScripture.why: Jesus promises another Helper, of the same kind as himself, to be with the disciples forever, and says the Spirit dwells with them and will be in them, naming the Spirit not as a force dispatched from far off but as a personal presence, God himself, who comes to live inside the people of God.

discussion.q: Before tonight, if someone had asked you who the Holy Spirit is, what would you honestly have said, and how does that compare to how you would describe the Father and the Son?
discussion.behind: Surface the gap before correcting it. Most people can describe the Father and the Son and go vague on the Spirit, and naming that out loud is the whole point of the opening. Do not rush to fix it. Let the room feel the size of what has been missing, and go first if it is slow.

discussion.q: Bell says we treat the Spirit as a force, an it, a kind of divine power we switch on. Where have you caught yourself thinking of the Spirit as a thing God uses rather than as God himself?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the it. We say things like the Spirit fell or I felt the Spirit in a way we would never say of the Father. The aim is to notice the grammar of our own forgetting, gently, so people see they have been worshiping a vapor without meaning to.

discussion.q: Scripture says the Spirit can be grieved, lied to, and resisted. What does it change to know that only a person can be grieved, that you can wound the Spirit the way you wound someone who loves you?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. The personhood of the Spirit is not a doctrine for its own sake, it is a relationship. Help the room feel that grieving the Spirit is not tripping a circuit but hurting Someone, which is both more sobering and more tender than the force model allows.

discussion.q: Bell says the reason we forget the Spirit is not that he is unimportant but that he is humble, that he points away from himself to Christ. How does that reframe his apparent quietness?
discussion.behind: Protect against the overcorrection. The Spirit's self-effacement is not absence, it is character. The aim is to help the room stop reading the Spirit's lack of self-promotion as a reason to ignore him and start reading it as the very thing it is, a person who delights to glorify another.

discussion.q: Bell admits he can preach the Trinity and then pray and live as though the Spirit were not in the room. Where have you held the doctrine on paper while functionally living as though God were distant?
discussion.behind: Move from teaching to self-implication. You are not hunting confession. You want each person, the leader first, to admit the gap between the creed they affirm and the absence they live. Go first. The honesty here opens the rest of the study.

objections.objection: The Spirit is the power of God, plainly, the energy that fills believers and makes things happen. Calling him a person is reading too much into poetic language about wind and fire and breath.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. The Spirit is power, Scripture says so, and the images of wind and fire and living water are not nothing, they tell us he fills and moves and gives life. Then make the distinction with care. The same Scripture that uses those images also says Ananias lied to the Spirit, that the Ephesians could grieve the Spirit, that Stephen's hearers always resisted the Spirit. You cannot lie to electricity. You cannot grieve the wind. You can only lie to and grieve and resist a someone. The Spirit is called the Helper, he teaches, he intercedes, he wills, he speaks, he can be blasphemed in a way that is unforgivable. A force does none of that. The power is real, but the power belongs to a person, and to keep the power while losing the person is to keep the gift and lose the Giver.

objections.objection: All this talk of the Spirit as a personal presence inside you is exactly what leads to the emotionalism and the chaos I have seen, people chasing feelings and calling every impulse the Spirit. Better to keep him safely in the doctrine of God and not let it get strange.
objections.response: Grant what is right, because much of it is. Real harm has been done in the Spirit's name, impulses baptized as guidance, manipulation dressed as anointing, a hunger for experience that left people exhausted and deceived. A proper fear of that is healthy. Then press the other edge gently. To wall the Spirit off in the doctrine of God so he never touches your actual life is its own deep error, because the Spirit Jesus promised was not a clause in a creed but a presence to be with us and in us forever. The answer to bad experience is not no experience. It is the Spirit tested by the Word, the same Spirit who inspired Scripture never contradicting it. Do not chase every feeling. But do not exile the living God to a footnote because some have abused his name. Honor the Word. Do not erase the presence.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the Holy Spirit is a person who can be grieved, when did you last consider that the way you have lived might have wounded Someone who loves you, rather than merely broken a rule?
sessions.practice: This week, change one word in how you pray. When you would normally end a prayer by mentioning the Spirit at the close, or skip him entirely, instead begin once a day by speaking to the Spirit directly and simply, as a person who is present. Holy Spirit, you are here. Help me. Do not perform anything. Just practice addressing the God who indwells you as the someone he is, and write down whether speaking to him rather than about him changed anything.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we confess that we have known your Son and called on your name and left your Spirit a stranger, a power we used and a person we forgot. Forgive us for grieving the One we treated as a force. You are God, of one being with the Father and the Son, and you have come to live in us, and we have lived as though the house were empty. Open our eyes to the presence we have ignored. Holy Spirit, humble and quiet, pointing always to Christ, we welcome you, not as a feeling we chase but as the God who is already here. Amen.
reflection: Where have I worshiped two persons of the Trinity and left the third a vapor, and what has that cost me without my noticing?
If the Spirit can be grieved, what in my life this week has grieved Someone rather than merely tripped a rule?
What would change if I lived all day as though God were not far above me but living inside me, present in the next ordinary moment?
sessions.teaching: Start with the test most of us would fail. Ask a roomful of lifelong Christians to describe the Father, and they will manage it. Ask them to describe the Son, and they will do better still, because they have a face, a life, a cross. Then ask them who the Holy Spirit is, and watch the pause. Something about a power. A feeling. An influence. A force that comes over you in worship. Francis Chan named a whole book after this, the forgotten God, and the title is an accusation we have earned, because what we have done is not lose a doctrine. We have lost a person of the Godhead. We have reduced God himself to a vapor, and we did it so quietly we never noticed the room had gone empty. So we do not begin with what the Spirit does, which is where everyone wants to begin, hungry for power or gifts or guidance. We begin with the harder question. Who is he. Take the two errors that pull against each other, and take them at full strength. The first treats the Spirit as a force, an it, a divine electricity that fills you and lights you up and makes you feel the presence of God. And there is a true instinct buried in it. The Spirit really is power. He really does fill. The images Scripture gives are not decoration, the rushing wind at Pentecost, the tongues of fire, the living water, the breath of God. To strip all of that out and leave a bloodless abstraction is to miss something true. The second error runs the other way, so frightened of emotionalism and chaos that it files the Spirit safely under the doctrine of God, affirmed in the creed, absent from the week, true on paper and functionally dead. And there is a true instinct there too, a proper fear of a faith that becomes a hunt for sensations and calls every impulse divine guidance. Now watch what happens when neither error is allowed to win the whole field. The Spirit is not a force, which destroys the first position, and the proof is devastatingly simple. Scripture says the Spirit can be grieved. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, Paul writes. It says Ananias lied to the Spirit and fell down dead. It says Stephen's accusers always resisted the Spirit, as their fathers did. Now think about what those verbs require. You cannot grieve electricity. You cannot lie to the wind. You cannot resist a feeling in the way you resist a someone pressing on your conscience. To grieve, to lie to, to resist, these are things you can only do to a person. The Spirit teaches. He intercedes. He wills, distributing gifts as he wills. He speaks, set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. He can be blasphemed, and that blasphemy alone Jesus calls unforgivable, which makes no sense at all if the Spirit is an impersonal power. Think for a moment about what it means to grieve someone, because we have flattened that word too. You do not grieve a stranger. You grieve someone who loves you, someone whose face changes when you wound them, someone close enough that what you do reaches them. Paul is telling us that the God who indwells us is near enough and personal enough to be hurt by how we live, not as a rule is broken but as a relationship is bruised, and the moment you feel the difference between tripping a wire and wounding a friend, the whole force model of the Spirit collapses in your hands. But the Spirit is also not a footnote, which destroys the second position, because the presence Jesus actually promised was not a clause in a doctrine of God. He said he would ask the Father, and the Father would give them another Helper, to be with them forever. That word another matters. It means another of the same kind as Jesus himself, a personal presence, not a downgrade to an influence. And he says this Helper, who has been with you, will be in you. With and in. Not an energy dispatched from a safe distance but God himself coming to live inside the people of God. So here is the verdict, and the leader must hold it cleanly. The Spirit is God, of one being with the Father and the Son, not a created power but the third person of the one God. He is personal, he speaks and wills and loves and grieves. And he is here, indwelling, nearer to you than your own breath, because the word for Spirit is the word for breath. Then the question that should trouble us. If he is God, present, personal, indwelling, why on earth do we forget him. And the answer is not that he is unimportant. The answer is that he is humble. The Spirit does not point to himself. When the Spirit of truth comes, Jesus said, he will not speak on his own authority, he will glorify me. The Spirit's whole delight is to turn the spotlight onto Christ and stay in the shadows himself, and we, trained to notice only what promotes itself, mistook his self-effacement for absence. We thought the quiet one was the unimportant one. That is the world's logic, where the one who promotes himself loudest is judged to matter most, and we carried that logic straight into our reading of God and concluded that the person who never demands the spotlight must be the lesser one. We could not have been more wrong. And I have to stand inside this, because I can preach the Trinity on a Sunday, all three persons, fully God, and then pray that same afternoon as though I were shouting up at a distant sky, and live the whole week as though the house were empty, as though the God who raised Jesus from the dead were not at that moment dwelling in me. The forgetting is not only theirs. It is mine. The Spirit has been in the room the entire time, the humble person of the Godhead, glorifying Christ and waiting, with a patience that itself should break us, to be known.

scriptureStudy.note: Jesus promises another Helper to be with them forever, the Spirit of truth who dwells with them and will be in them. Another means another of the same kind, a person like Jesus, not an influence, and with and in name a presence, not a distant power.

Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed. You cannot grieve a force. The command assumes a person who feels, who can be wounded by how his people live, which is the death of the it model of the Spirit.

Peter tells Ananias he has lied to the Holy Spirit, and then that he has not lied to men but to God. In one breath the Spirit is named as the one lied to and as God, settling both the personhood and the deity at once.

All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills. The Spirit wills and chooses and distributes, the action of a person with a mind, not the discharge of an impersonal power.

The Holy Spirit said, set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. The Spirit speaks, calls, and claims a work as his own, the speech of a person, not the hum of a current.

The Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. From the first page the Spirit is present and active in creation itself, no latecomer to the story but God at work before there was anyone to feel him.

Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. The Spirit is the mark of belonging to God, his indwelling the very thing that makes you Christ's, which is impossible if he is merely an optional power for special believers.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long fight the church had to have to say what it finally said about the Spirit, because we did not arrive at the personhood and the deity of the Spirit by reflex. In the centuries after the apostles, the church wrestled hard, and a party arose, the ones Athanasius and others called the Spirit-fighters, who were willing to grant that the Spirit was something more than a creature but balked at calling him fully God. Read against that backdrop the work of Athanasius and the Cappadocian fathers, especially Basil of Caesarea, whose treatise on the Holy Spirit argued that the Spirit must be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, which only makes sense if the Spirit is God. The Council of Constantinople in 381 settled it, expanding the creed to confess the Spirit as the Lord and giver of life, who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified. A serious group should weigh why this mattered so much that the church would not let it go. If the Spirit who indwells you is not fully God, then God does not actually live in you, only a creature does, and your salvation is mediated by something less than God himself. The deity of the Spirit is not a technicality. It is the difference between God present and a messenger sent. Set this beside the modern habit of vague spirituality, the talk of energy and presence and the universe, and ask what is lost when the Spirit becomes a feeling again rather than the Lord and giver of life the church bled to confess. The discipline of this whole study is to refuse to relax that confession, to hold that the One who lives in us is God, personal, and worthy of the same worship we give the Father and the Son.

memoryVerse.text: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.

sessions.title: Born of the Spirit
sessions.aim: To take the new birth as the Spirit's work and not ours, to see regeneration as God raising the spiritually dead rather than coaching the spiritually struggling, and to let the writer's own conversion from atheism stand as evidence that the Spirit does what argument never could.
sessions.summary: Jesus tells a religious expert, a man who had done everything right, that none of it counts, that he must be born again, born of the Spirit, or he will never even see the kingdom. The first question is why Jesus aims the hardest words about regeneration not at the worst sinner in the room but at the most respectable man in Israel. The answer is that the new birth is not improvement. It is resurrection. You do not contribute to your own birth, the first one or the second, and Nicodemus, who can do many things, cannot do this. Bell takes the strong form of the objection, that conversion is just a decision a person makes, that you choose to believe and the choosing is yours, and he grants the real thing under it, that we do believe, do repent, do come, really and responsibly. But he will not let the human decision swallow the divine act. The Spirit is the wind, Jesus says, blowing where it wills, and you hear it but cannot command it. Bell stands inside this with his own story, because he was an atheist, certain, intelligent, unmoved by the arguments he had heard and answered. What changed him was not a better syllogism. He was made alive by a presence he had no category for, and he knows, all the way down, that he did not author it. Then the turn. If the new birth is the Spirit's work, then no one is beyond it, not the hardest skeptic, not the most cynical heart, because the same Spirit who hovered over the waters and raised Christ from the tomb is in the business of making the dead alive, and the dead do not improve their way to life. They are raised.

keyScripture.why: Jesus tells Nicodemus that unless one is born of water and the Spirit he cannot enter the kingdom of God, that flesh gives birth to flesh but the Spirit gives birth to spirit, and that the Spirit is like the wind that blows where it wishes, naming the new birth as the sovereign work of God and not the achievement of the one being born.

discussion.q: Jesus tells the most respectable, religious man in Israel that he must be born again. Why do you think the hardest words about needing a new birth land on the good man and not the obvious sinner?
discussion.behind: Open on the surprise. We expect the call to be born again to go to the prostitute and the tax collector. Jesus aims it at the Pharisee. The aim is to expose the assumption that respectability is a head start toward God, and to feel that the new birth levels everyone, the moral and the immoral alike.

discussion.q: Bell says the new birth is not improvement but resurrection, that you contribute to your second birth exactly as much as you contributed to your first, which is nothing. How does that sit with you?
discussion.behind: Press on the image. We are deeply committed to the idea that we did something to get saved. The aim is to feel the offense and the relief of the birth metaphor together, that a baby does not assist in being born, and to let that reframe what conversion actually is.

discussion.q: Bell takes the objection that conversion is simply a decision we make. What is true in that, and what does it miss about the Spirit being the wind that blows where it wills?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully. We really do decide, believe, repent, and the leader must not deny human responsibility. The miss is treating the decision as the whole cause. Help the room hold the mystery, that we truly choose and the Spirit truly raises, without flattening either side.

discussion.q: Bell was an atheist who had heard the arguments and answered them, and what finally changed him was not a better argument but a presence. If conversion were only about being persuaded, what would be missing?
discussion.behind: Get the room to feel the limit of argument. Many think the unconverted just need the right case made. The aim is to recognize that information does not raise the dead, that the writer was not out-argued but made alive, which changes how we pray for the people we love.

discussion.q: If the new birth is the Spirit's work and not the sinner's achievement, how should that change the way you pray for the hardest, most cynical person you know?
discussion.behind: Close on hope and self-implication. We give up on people we judge too far gone, which secretly assumes their salvation depends on their openness rather than the Spirit's power. Invite the room to name that person and to pray differently. Go first.

objections.objection: Conversion is just a decision a person makes. You weigh the evidence, you choose to believe, and the choosing is yours. All this talk of the Spirit raising the dead takes away human freedom and makes us puppets.
objections.response: Bell grants the real thing under this. We do decide. The gospel says believe, and repent, and come, and means it, and the one who comes is genuinely responsible for coming and the one who refuses is genuinely responsible for refusing. None of that is denied. Then mark what the decision cannot account for. Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to decide harder, he tells him he must be born again, born of the Spirit, and births are not things you perform on yourself. The dead do not choose to rise, they are raised, and Paul says we were dead in our trespasses before God made us alive. The mystery the church has always held is that the same act is fully the Spirit's work and truly your response, the wind that blows where it wills and the sail that genuinely catches it. To collapse it into only your decision is to make yourself the author of your own resurrection, which no one who has actually been raised believes for a moment.

objections.objection: If the new birth is entirely the Spirit's sovereign work and blows where it wills, then why evangelize at all, and why is it the sinner's fault if he is not chosen to be born again?
objections.response: Hold this honestly, because it is the oldest hard question and the leader should not pretend it away. First, on evangelism, notice that the Spirit ordinarily works through the Word being spoken, faith comes by hearing, so the sovereignty of the Spirit is not a reason for silence but the only reason our words have any power at all, since we cannot raise the dead and he can. We speak because he works through speaking. Second, on fault, Scripture refuses to let the sinner off the hook, no one resists God because he was forbidden to come, every refusal is a real and willing refusal, and every person who comes finds they are welcomed. The Bible holds the Spirit's freedom and the sinner's responsibility together without resolving the tension into a system, and a study that respects the text will resist the urge to relieve the discomfort by denying one side.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you are honest, do you believe you contributed something decisive to your own salvation, or have you ever once stood before the fact that you were dead and Someone made you alive without your permission?
sessions.practice: This week, write down the story of how you came to faith, or how you are still coming, in plain words, and as you write, mark every place where you can see Someone working on you before you ever moved toward God. The conversation you did not seek. The verse that would not leave you. The grief that softened you. Do not credit yourself with the parts that were the wind. If you cannot find your own story yet, write the name of the person whose conversion you most long for, and pray for the wind to blow there.
sessions.closingPrayer: God who hovered over the waters and raised your Son from the tomb, we were dead and you made us alive, and we did nothing to deserve it and nothing to accomplish it. Forgive us for taking the credit, for treating the new birth as our clever decision rather than your sovereign mercy. We thank you for every soul in this room you raised, for the writer you found when he was certain you did not exist, and we ask you to blow again, here, on the hardest hearts we know and on our own cold places. You are the Lord and giver of life. Give it. Amen.
reflection: When I tell the story of my faith, who is the main actor, and is that honest?
Where in my coming to Christ can I now see the Spirit working on me before I ever turned toward God?
Whom have I quietly given up on as too far gone, and what does the new birth as resurrection say about that verdict?
sessions.teaching: Jesus has a night conversation with a man named Nicodemus, and everything about the setup tells you to expect a gentle word. Nicodemus is a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, a teacher of Israel, a man who has kept the law and studied the Scriptures and done, by every visible measure, everything right. He comes respectfully, calling Jesus a teacher come from God. And Jesus, instead of commending him, says the hardest thing he ever says to anyone about salvation. Truly, truly, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God. Sit with where that lands. The demand for a new birth is aimed not at the worst sinner in the city but at the best man in the room, and that is the first thing we have to feel, because it dismantles the lie we all carry, that respectability is a head start with God, that the moral man is closer to the kingdom than the immoral one. Jesus says no. The good man and the bad man need the identical thing, and it is not improvement. It is birth. And if anything, the respectable man is in greater danger, because his decency is a better disguise. The obvious sinner at least knows he is in trouble. The good man has spent his whole life building a case that he is fine, and the harder that case is to argue against, the harder it is for him to hear that he must be born again, that everything he has stacked up counts for nothing in the one matter that decides everything. Nicodemus hears it and is baffled in exactly the right way. How can a man be born when he is old. Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb. He has stumbled onto the offense without understanding it, because the offense is real. Birth is the one thing in the universe you absolutely cannot do for yourself. You did not assist in your first birth. You did not decide it, plan it, cooperate with it, or contribute to it in the smallest degree. You were not consulted. You were brought into being by another, entirely. And Jesus is saying the second birth is exactly like the first in this respect. Flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit gives birth to spirit. The new birth is not the old self improved, educated, or persuaded. It is a dead thing made alive, and the dead contribute nothing to their own resurrection. Now take the objection at full strength, because it is the honest one and most of us feel it. Surely conversion is a decision. You hear the gospel, you weigh it, you choose to believe, and the choice is yours. And Bell grants the real thing under this, fully. We do decide. The gospel commands belief and repentance and means them, and the man who comes really comes and the man who refuses really refuses, and no one is dragged kicking into the kingdom against a will that wanted nothing to do with it. The Scriptures hold human responsibility everywhere and never apologize for it. But watch the thing the decision cannot explain, because Jesus puts it right in front of us. The wind blows where it wishes, he says, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit. The Spirit is the wind. You do not summon the wind. You do not command it, schedule it, or manufacture it. You feel it when it comes, you see what it does, but it blows on its own authority, where it wills, and the new birth is like that. Truly your response, and truly his work, the sail that genuinely catches the wind and the wind that was never yours to produce. And here I have to put my own story on the table, because this is not abstract for me. I was an atheist. Not a casual one, a convinced one. I had heard the arguments for God and I had answers for them, and the answers were not stupid, and the people making the arguments rarely moved me, because you do not argue a dead man into breathing. I was not waiting for better evidence. I was, in the language of Scripture, dead in my trespasses, and a dead man does not know he is dead, and cannot want to be otherwise. What changed me was not a syllogism. It was not a debate I lost. It was a presence I had no category for, a wind that began to blow on a man who had not asked for it and could not have produced it, and when I came to faith I knew, all the way down in a place arguments do not reach, that I had not done this. I had been done unto. I was raised. I still cannot fully explain it, and the inability to explain it is itself part of the evidence, because you cannot explain a wind you did not call. So here is the turn, and it is the most hopeful thing in this whole session. If the new birth is the Spirit's work and not the sinner's achievement, then no one you love is beyond it. Not the hardest skeptic. Not the cynic who has heard it all. Not the one who has answers for every argument you could make, because the answer was never an argument. The same Spirit who hovered over the dark waters at the beginning, the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead, is in the business of making dead things alive, and the dead do not improve their way to life across some gradual slope of persuasion. They are raised, suddenly, by a power outside themselves, the way I was raised, the way you were raised if you have been. So we do not give up on people because they seem too far gone, because too far gone is the only condition the Spirit has ever worked with. We were all that. And we pray for the wind, and we speak the Word the wind blows through, and we wait for the God who calls the dead by name.

scriptureStudy.note: Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God. Not improved, not reformed, born. And the demand is aimed at the most religious man in Israel, leveling the respectable and the ruined at a stroke.

That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and the Spirit is like the wind blowing where it wishes. The new birth is the Spirit's sovereign work, felt and seen in its effects but never summoned or controlled by the one being born.

I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you, and I will put my Spirit within you. Centuries before Nicodemus, God promised regeneration as his own act, removing the heart of stone, the new birth as a divine transplant, not a human effort.

Even when we were dead in our trespasses, God made us alive together with Christ. The starting condition is death, and the dead do not cooperate. Made us alive names the new birth as resurrection, accomplished by God on the spiritually dead.

He saved us by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit. Salvation is tied directly to the Spirit's renewing work, not to our righteous deeds, which Paul explicitly excludes as the cause.

He has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The new birth is something he caused, the cause lying in God's mercy and Christ's resurrection, not in the merit of the one born again.

Children of God, born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. John rules out every human source of the new birth in a single line, leaving God alone as its author.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the old and unresolved conversation about the order of salvation, because the new birth raises a question the church has never stopped debating, namely whether regeneration precedes faith or faith precedes regeneration, whether the Spirit makes you alive so that you can believe or your believing is the occasion of being made alive. Read the Reformed tradition, with Augustine behind it, arguing that the dead cannot believe until they are first made alive, so the Spirit's regenerating work comes first and faith is its fruit, and set it honestly beside the traditions that stress the genuine and decisive responsibility of the human will to respond, fearing that to make regeneration entirely prior is to reduce the sinner to a passive object. A serious group should resist the urge to score the debate quickly, and should instead notice what every side affirms, that salvation is finally of the Lord, that no one boasts before God, that the new birth is grace and not wage. The discipline is to hold the mystery the way Scripture holds it, refusing both the error that makes God a spectator waiting on human permission and the error that makes the human being a puppet with no real response. Weigh as well the pastoral stakes, because how you answer shapes how you evangelize and how you pray, and consider why the writer, an atheist made alive, found in his own experience a stronger witness to the priority of grace than any argument supplied, since he knows he did not begin the thing that saved him. The aim is not to win the old fight in one session but to come away certain of the one thing all sides confess, that the One who began a good work in you will bring it to completion, because he began it.

memoryVerse.text: That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Do not marvel that I said to you, you must be born again.

sessions.title: The Fruit and the Walk
sessions.aim: To take the fruit of the Spirit as the slow growth of a real change worked from the inside, not a list of behaviors to manufacture, and to draw the hard line between fruit that the Spirit produces and performance that we produce to be seen.
sessions.summary: Paul lists nine things and calls them the fruit of the Spirit, and the first thing to notice is the word fruit, singular, and the word Spirit. Not the works of the believer. The fruit of the Spirit. The first question is the difference between fruit and performance, because both can look identical from the outside, and the church is full of people exhausted from manufacturing what was only ever meant to grow. Bell takes the strong form of two errors. The first says sanctification is all effort, grit your teeth, try harder, white-knuckle your way to holiness, and there is a true thing under it, that Scripture really does command us to put sin to death and to walk by the Spirit, that passivity is not the answer. The second says it is all passive, let go and let God, and there is a true thing there too, that we cannot produce fruit by straining, that a branch does not grunt to grow apples. Bell refuses both. The fruit is not manufactured, which refutes the first, because a tree does not perform fruit, it bears it out of what it is. And the fruit is not automatic, which refutes the second, because Paul commands a walk, a daily keeping in step, an active putting to death of the flesh. The resolution is the branch and the vine. You do not produce the fruit and you do not produce it by doing nothing. You abide, you stay connected, you keep walking in step with the Spirit, and the fruit comes slowly, unevenly, more like a season than a switch. Then the turn. Bell names his own decades, the sins he assumed grace would have removed by now and has not, and tells the truth the church hides, that sanctification is slow, that the impatience to be done with it is itself a refusal to walk. The fruit grows at the speed of a tree. We wanted it at the speed of a purchase.

keyScripture.why: Paul calls love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control the fruit of the Spirit, and then says if we live by the Spirit let us also keep in step with the Spirit, naming the change as the Spirit's produce and our part as a daily walking in step rather than a manufacturing of results.

discussion.q: Paul calls it the fruit of the Spirit, not the works of the believer. What changes when you hear your growth in love or patience as something grown in you rather than something achieved by you?
discussion.behind: Open on the grammar. We instinctively hear the list as a to-do list and grind ourselves against it. The aim is to relocate the source from our effort to the Spirit's work, so the room can begin to tell the difference between bearing fruit and manufacturing it.

discussion.q: Bell says fruit and performance can look identical from the outside. Where have you produced the appearance of a virtue, kindness or patience, while inside it was effort to be seen and not the Spirit's work?
discussion.behind: Press gently into self-examination, not shame. We all perform virtues we do not possess. The aim is honest recognition that polished behavior can be empty, and that the Spirit grows the real thing slowly while performance produces the fake thing fast.

discussion.q: Bell takes both errors, that sanctification is all gritted effort and that it is all let go and let God. Which one are you more tempted by, and what is true in the one you resist?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Strivers need to hear about abiding, passives need to hear about the walk and the putting to death. The aim is for each person to find their own imbalance and to receive the true thing in the error they are tempted to despise.

discussion.q: Bell admits there are sins he assumed grace would have removed by now and has not. Where has the slowness of your own change tempted you to give up or to fake it?
discussion.behind: This is the tender center. The slowness of sanctification disillusions people and drives them to performance or despair. The aim is to normalize the slowness, to feel that fruit grows at the speed of a tree, and to keep walking. Go first and be specific.

discussion.q: Jesus says apart from him you can do nothing, and Paul says keep in step with the Spirit. How do you hold abiding and walking together without collapsing into either pure passivity or pure effort?
discussion.behind: Close on the both-and. The branch image holds it, you stay connected and you keep walking, neither straining to produce nor drifting in neutral. Help the room name one concrete way they will both abide and walk this week, rather than choosing one.

objections.objection: This fruit language is just a softer way of saying try harder. At the end of the day I still have to produce love and patience and self-control, so calling it fruit is a comforting word for the same exhausting demand.
objections.response: Bell grants the part that is true, that Scripture really does command effort, that Paul says put to death what is earthly in you and walk by the Spirit, and that anyone waiting passively for holiness to arrive will wait forever. The demand is real. Then mark the difference the word fruit makes. A branch does work in a sense, it stays on the vine, it does not break itself off, but it does not strain to produce the apple, the apple is the natural overflow of being connected to the life of the vine. Your effort is not the effort of manufacturing the virtue by willpower. It is the effort of staying connected, of keeping in step, of putting yourself in the way of the Spirit's work through prayer and the Word and obedience. You labor at abiding. The fruit itself grows from the life you are joined to, and that is why two people can do the identical good deed and one bears fruit while the other only performs, because one is connected to the vine and the other is straining alone.

objections.objection: If the fruit is the Spirit's work and grows slowly on its own, then I can stop trying and just wait for it. Let go and let God. My job is to relax and let the Spirit do everything.
objections.response: No, and Paul closes the door on this in the same passage, so we should too. Right after listing the fruit he says those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, and then commands, let us keep in step with the Spirit. Keep in step is a walking word, an active, deliberate, daily matching of your pace to another's. There is nothing passive about it. The let go and let God instinct is right that you cannot manufacture fruit by gritting your teeth, but it is wrong that you therefore do nothing, because abiding is not idleness. The branch that abides is doing the most active thing it can do, refusing to detach, staying in the place where life flows. You put sin to death actively, you walk actively, and you trust the fruit to the Spirit. Effort, yes. Effort to abide and to walk, not effort to produce by force what only the Spirit can grow.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What virtue have you been performing for others while knowing, in the quiet, that the inside does not match the outside, and what would it mean to stop performing it and ask the Spirit to grow the real thing?
sessions.practice: This week, pick the one piece of the fruit you most lack, the one that is hardest for you, patience maybe, or self-control, or kindness. Do not try to manufacture it by willpower. Instead, each day name it to the Spirit honestly, I do not have this, please grow it in me, and then put yourself in the way of the work, in prayer, in Scripture, in the next ordinary chance to practice it. At the end of the week, write down not how much you produced but where you saw the smallest green shoot you did not force.
sessions.closingPrayer: Spirit of God, we have tried to manufacture what only you can grow, and we are tired from the performance, and ashamed of how little of the real thing there is in us after all these years. Forgive our impatience, and forgive the fake fruit we hung on dead branches to be admired. Keep us connected to the Vine. Teach us to walk in step with you, neither straining as though it depended on us alone nor drifting as though we had nothing to do. Grow your fruit in us at whatever slow speed is true, and give us the patience to keep walking while it comes. Amen.
reflection: Which am I more tempted by, the exhaustion of trying to manufacture holiness or the drift of waiting passively for it, and what is the true thing in the error I resist?
Where has the slowness of my own change tempted me to give up, to fake it, or to conclude the gospel does not work?
What does it mean, concretely, this week, for me both to abide in the Vine and to keep in step with the Spirit?
sessions.teaching: Paul gives us a list we have all heard so often it has gone smooth, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control, and we read it as a checklist of behaviors to muster. But look at what he calls it before he lists a single item. The fruit of the Spirit. Not the works of the believer. Not the achievements of the disciplined Christian. The fruit of the Spirit, and every word in that phrase matters. Fruit, not product. And of the Spirit, not of you. Because the great confusion of the Christian life is that fruit and performance look identical from the outside, and the church is packed with people worn down to the bone from manufacturing what was only ever meant to grow. So the question for this session is the difference between the two, between fruit that is borne and performance that is produced, because if you cannot tell them apart in your own life you will spend your years exhausted and faking it and wondering why holiness feels like a treadmill. Take the two errors at full strength, because most of us live in one of them. The first says sanctification is effort, plain and hard. Grit your teeth. Try harder. White-knuckle your way toward holiness by sheer determination, and if you are not growing it is because you are not trying enough. And there is a true thing buried in it that we dare not lose, because Scripture really does command effort. Paul says put to death what is earthly in you. He says walk by the Spirit. He says work out your salvation. The man waiting passively for holiness to descend on him like weather will wait until he dies. Passivity is a lie. But the second error runs the other way and says it is all passive, let go and let God, stop trying, just relax and let the Spirit do everything while you rest. And there is a true thing in that one too, because you genuinely cannot manufacture the fruit by straining. A branch does not grunt and strain to produce an apple. No amount of willpower has ever squeezed real patience out of an impatient heart. So both errors hold a truth and both, alone, are deadly. Now watch the resolution, because Jesus gave it before Paul ever wrote the list, in the image of the vine and the branches. I am the vine, he said, you are the branches. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me. Apart from me you can do nothing. There it is. The fruit is not manufactured, which kills the first error, because a branch does not perform fruit by effort, it bears fruit as the natural overflow of being joined to the life of the vine. And the fruit is not automatic, which kills the second error, because the branch has one urgent, active, ceaseless task, to abide, to stay connected, to refuse to detach. And Paul says the same thing at the end of his list in the plainest terms. If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit. Keep in step. That is a walking word, a marching word, the deliberate matching of your stride to someone else's pace, and there is nothing passive in it. Notice the order Paul gives, because it guards both errors at once. If we live by the Spirit, that is the first thing, the life is already given, you do not generate it, you were made alive by the Spirit and you live by him. And then, let us also keep in step. The walking does not produce the life. The life produces the walking. You do not march in order to be made alive. You were made alive, and so now you march, matching your pace to the Spirit who is already moving. The man who tries to keep in step before he has the life is just performing, and the man who has the life and refuses to keep in step is just drifting, and Paul will allow neither. You do not produce the fruit, and you do not produce it by doing nothing. You abide and you walk. You stay connected to the Vine through prayer and the Word and the fellowship of the saints, and you keep deliberately in step with the Spirit through obedience and the active putting to death of the flesh, and out of that connected, walking life the fruit grows, slowly, unevenly, in seasons, the way fruit has always grown. And here is where I have to tell the truth the church works hard to hide, because I am decades into this now and there are sins in me I genuinely assumed grace would have removed by this point, and it has not, not yet, not all the way. There are patterns I have brought to God a thousand times that are smaller than they were and not gone. And the temptation, when the change is that slow, is one of two things, either to give up and conclude the whole thing does not work, or to start faking it, to perform the patience I do not have and hang plastic fruit on a branch that is not bearing, so that at least it looks alive. Both are a refusal to walk. Because there is something about fruit that our whole impatient age cannot stand. It grows at the speed of a tree. You plant, you water, you wait through seasons that look like nothing is happening, and the growth is real but it is slow, and you cannot rush it any more than you can pull a seedling taller with your hands. We wanted sanctification at the speed of a purchase, instant, complete, paid for and delivered. God gives it at the speed of a harvest. And the patience to keep walking while the fruit comes slowly is itself, you will notice, one of the nine. The Spirit grows the very thing the slow growing requires. So do not give up, and do not fake it. Stay on the Vine. Keep in step. And trust the Gardener, who has never once abandoned a tree he planted, to bring the fruit in its season.

scriptureStudy.note: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. The command is a walk, active and ongoing, and the promise is that the way to defeat the flesh is not direct combat alone but a positive walking with the Spirit.
The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, and the rest. Fruit, singular, and of the Spirit, so the nine are one cluster grown by one source, not nine separate achievements of the disciplined will.

Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, so let us keep in step with the Spirit. Paul joins an active putting to death of sin to a deliberate keeping in step, closing the door on the passivity that hears fruit and stops trying.

Abide in me, for apart from me you can do nothing. The branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine, which holds together the two truths, that you cannot produce it yourself and that you must actively remain connected.

He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. The slowness is not abandonment. The same God who started the change guarantees its finish, on his timetable, not ours.

We are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. The change is gradual, degree by degree, and it is done to us by the Spirit, named here as the Lord who does the transforming.

If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. Notice the joining, by the Spirit you put to death, neither pure effort nor pure passivity but your action carried by his power.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian wisdom on the means of grace, because the abiding and the walking that this session calls for are not vague spiritual moods but have always had concrete shape, and recovering that shape protects the fruit from both errors. The tradition has spoken of ordinary means through which the Spirit ordinarily works, the reading and hearing of the Word, prayer, the Lord's Supper, the gathered worship of the church, and has insisted that while the Spirit is free, he has bound himself to work most often through these, so that to neglect them is to walk away from the very places the life flows. Read J. I. Packer, whose Keep in Step with the Spirit takes its title from this passage and argues for a sanctification that is neither the gritted self-effort of the moralist nor the passive let go and let God of a certain holiness teaching, but an active dependence, a strenuous trusting, that holds effort and grace together. Set this beside the modern hunger for instant change, the expectation shaped by a culture of quick results that healing and growth should be fast and felt, and ask what damage that expectation does to believers whose real but slow change leaves them feeling like failures. A serious group should weigh the older language of mortification and vivification, the putting to death of sin and the bringing to life of righteousness, as two sides of one Spirit-worked process, and should consider how the patience to endure slow growth is itself a fruit the Spirit grows, so that the waiting is not wasted time but part of the work. The discipline is to refuse the treadmill of performance and the hammock of passivity alike, and to take up instead the means of grace as the place where the branch stays joined to the Vine.

memoryVerse.text: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

sessions.title: Gifts and the Contested Question
sessions.aim: To put the continuationist and the cessationist cases at full and equal strength, to refuse to tell the group which is right, and to hold a room together in worship of the same Spirit across a divide that has split better Christians than us.
sessions.summary: The Spirit gives gifts, and the church has fought bitterly over which ones still operate. Do tongues, prophecy, and miraculous healing continue today, or did those sign gifts cease when the apostolic age closed and the Scriptures were completed. This session does the hard and unusual thing of refusing to settle it for the group, and instead puts both serious positions at their strongest, because both are held by faithful, careful, Christ-loving believers, and the divide does not run between the godly and the worldly. It runs through the middle of the godly. Bell presents the cessationist case at full strength, the argument that certain gifts authenticated the apostles and the giving of Scripture, that with the foundation laid and the canon closed those sign gifts had served their purpose, an argument carried by serious theologians like B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin, an argument that takes the sufficiency of Scripture with deadly seriousness and has watched real abuses with grief. Then he presents the continuationist case at full strength, the argument that the New Testament nowhere announces the gifts will cease before Christ returns, that Paul tells the Corinthians to eagerly desire them, that the burden of proof lies on the one claiming God stopped, an argument carried by serious theologians like Sam Storms and Gordon Fee, an argument that takes the present activity of the Spirit with deadly seriousness and has watched real cessationist deadness with grief. Bell will not break the tie. The first question is not who is right. It is whether the body of Christ can disagree about this without fracturing, whether we can hold the gifts loosely and the Spirit tightly. Then the turn. Paul, in the very chapter most quoted in this fight, interrupts the argument about gifts to write the greatest description of love ever penned, as if to say the gifts are real and the gifts are not the point, that a church right about cessation or continuation and wrong about love is a clanging gong. The verdict is not a position. It is a posture.

keyScripture.why: Paul says there are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit, varieties of service but the same Lord, and that to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good, grounding every gift in one Giver and one purpose, the building up of the body, which is the common ground beneath the contested question of which gifts continue.

discussion.q: Before tonight, where did you land on whether gifts like tongues and prophecy and healing continue today, and where did that conviction come from, study, experience, or the tradition you were raised in?
discussion.behind: Surface the room's starting positions and their sources honestly. Many hold a view they inherited rather than examined. The aim is not to change minds yet but to expose that our convictions here often come from background and experience, which builds humility before the arguments arrive.

discussion.q: The cessationist argues that certain gifts authenticated the apostles and the closing of Scripture, and so served their purpose and ceased. Stated at its strongest, what is genuinely compelling in that case?
discussion.behind: Make the room build the cessationist case fairly, including the continuationists in the room. The aim is the discipline of steelmanning, that you must be able to state the other side so well its holders would agree. Do not let it be caricatured as mere unbelief.

discussion.q: The continuationist argues that the New Testament never announces the gifts will cease before Christ returns and tells us to eagerly desire them. Stated at its strongest, what is genuinely compelling in that case?
discussion.behind: Now make the room build the continuationist case just as fairly, including the cessationists. The aim is the same discipline in the other direction. Hold the two strong cases side by side so the room feels the weight of both and the ease of neither.

discussion.q: Bell refuses to break the tie and tell us who is right. Does that frustrate you, and what does it reveal about how tightly we want to hold a position the Bible itself leaves more open than we do?
discussion.behind: Press on the discomfort of unsettledness. We want a verdict. The aim is to examine our own need to be certain where Scripture permits range, and to ask whether our certainty serves the body or our pride. Handle the strong feelings gently.

discussion.q: Paul interrupts the gifts chapters to write that without love the gifts are a clanging gong. If your group split over this question, what would it look like to be right about gifts and wrong about love?
discussion.behind: Close on the posture, which is the whole point. The aim is for the room to feel that fracturing over this would itself be the deeper failure, and to commit, out loud, to holding the Spirit tightly and the disputed question loosely. Go first, and name your own temptation to contempt.

objections.objection: The sign gifts have obviously ceased. Tongues and prophecy and miraculous healing belonged to the apostles, authenticating the foundation of the church and the giving of Scripture, and now that the foundation is laid and the canon is complete, we no longer need them. What passes for these gifts today is either psychological or counterfeit.
objections.response: Put this at full strength, because serious believers hold it for serious reasons. The cessationist case, carried by theologians like B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin, rests on real biblical observation. Certain gifts did cluster around the apostles and authenticate their unique role, miracles are tied in Scripture to confirming the message and its messengers, and the foundation, Paul says, was laid once by the apostles and prophets, not relaid in every generation. Beneath it is a precious commitment, the sufficiency of Scripture, a refusal to add fresh revelation to a closed and complete Word, and a grief over real abuses, the manipulation and the fakery done in the Spirit's name. A continuationist must grant all of this weight before answering it, must admit the abuses are real, must take the sufficiency of Scripture as seriously as the cessationist does, and must concede that nothing claimed today can stand alongside Scripture as new revelation. The cessationist is not an unbeliever afraid of the Spirit. He is often a careful exegete guarding something true.

objections.objection: The gifts obviously continue. Nowhere does the New Testament say they will stop before Christ returns, Paul plainly commands the Corinthians to earnestly desire the gifts including prophecy, and the same Spirit who gave them has not changed. To say God switched them off is to read a theory into a silence and to quench the Spirit the church is told never to quench.
objections.response: Put this at full strength too, because serious believers hold it for serious reasons. The continuationist case, carried by theologians like Sam Storms and Gordon Fee, rests on real biblical observation. Paul tells the Corinthians to earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that they may prophesy, and gives the church detailed instructions for ordering tongues and prophecy in worship, instructions that would be strange to leave in Scripture if they expired within a generation. The one passage often cited for cessation says the gifts will pass when the perfect comes, and continuationists argue the perfect is the return of Christ and the face to face seeing, not the closing of the canon. A cessationist must grant all of this weight before answering, must admit the New Testament contains no clear expiration date, must take the command to desire the gifts as seriously as the continuationist does, and must concede that to forbid what Scripture commands desiring is a heavy thing. The continuationist is not a thrill-seeker chasing experience. He is often a careful exegete refusing to silence a text.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: On this question where faithful Christians have long disagreed, is your certainty serving the unity of Christ's body, or is it serving your need to be right and to look down on those who differ?
sessions.practice: This week, do the harder of two things, depending on where you stand. If you are a settled cessationist, read one careful continuationist arguing the case at its best, and pray, Spirit, show me what is true in this that I have dismissed. If you are a settled continuationist, read one careful cessationist arguing the case at its best, and pray the same prayer. Whichever you are, write down one thing the other side sees that you had been too quick to wave away, and one place where your certainty has carried contempt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Holy Spirit, you give your gifts as you will, for the common good, and we have turned your gifts into a battlefield and your body into camps. Forgive us for the contempt we have carried toward brothers and sisters who love you and read the same Scriptures and land in a different place. Teach us to hold the disputed question with open hands and to hold you, and your church, and the love that outlasts every gift, with everything we have. Where we are wrong, correct us gently. Where we are right, keep us from pride. And make us, above all our arguing, a people known by love. Amen.
reflection: Where did my conviction about the gifts actually come from, careful study of Scripture, my own experience, or simply the tradition that raised me, and have I ever honestly examined the other side?
Can I state the position I disagree with so well that its holders would say yes, that is what we believe, and if not, what does that reveal?
Have I carried contempt toward believers who differ from me on this, and what would it cost me to hold the question loosely and the Spirit tightly?
sessions.teaching: We come now to the session most likely to make a room tense, and that is exactly why it must be handled with the most care, because the Spirit gives gifts and the church has spent a long time fighting over which of them still operate. The question is plain even if the answer is not. Do the gifts the New Testament calls tongues, prophecy, and miraculous healing continue in the church today, or did those particular sign gifts cease when the age of the apostles closed and the Scriptures were finished. And I am going to do something in this session that may frustrate you, because I am not going to tell you which side is right. That is not a dodge. It is a conviction, because this divide does not run between the faithful and the faithless, between the people who honor Scripture and the people who chase experience. It runs straight through the middle of the godly, and some of the most careful, Christ-loving, Bible-saturated believers I know land on opposite sides of it, and a study that pretended otherwise would be lying to you about the body of Christ. So I am going to do the harder thing. I am going to build both cases at full strength, the way each side would build it, and then I am going to refuse to break the tie, and then I am going to tell you what Paul does in the middle of the very chapters we fight over, which matters more than the tie ever did. Take the cessationist case first, and take it at its strongest, because it is strong. The argument runs like this. Certain gifts in the New Testament functioned to authenticate, to confirm that a true message was coming from a true messenger, and Scripture itself ties miracles to the confirming of the word, the signs of a true apostle. Those gifts clustered around the apostles in a way they did not cluster around ordinary believers, and the apostles had a unique, unrepeatable role, laying the foundation of the church and receiving and delivering the Scriptures. Paul says the household of God was built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, and a foundation is laid once. So the cessationist concludes that when the foundation was finished and the canon of Scripture was complete, the sign gifts that had served to authenticate the founders and the giving of revelation had done their work and ceased. Beneath the argument is something precious, a fierce commitment to the sufficiency of Scripture, a refusal to let anyone add fresh words from God to a finished Word, and behind that, real grief, because cessationists have watched manipulation and fakery and spiritual abuse done in the Spirit's name and have wanted to guard the flock from it. B. B. Warfield made this case with great force, and Richard Gaffin has made it carefully in our own time, and neither man is an unbeliever afraid of God. They are exegetes guarding something true. Now take the continuationist case, and take it at exactly the same strength, because it is just as strong. The argument runs like this. Nowhere, not in a single verse, does the New Testament announce that the gifts will switch off at some point before Christ returns. That is a striking silence, because the Scriptures speak often about the last days and the present age, and never once say the gifts belong only to a closing era. To the contrary, Paul commands the Corinthians to earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, and especially that they may prophesy, and he gives the church detailed, practical instructions for how to order tongues and prophecy in public worship, which is a strange thing to leave permanently in Scripture if those gifts were going to expire within a generation. The one text most often cited for cessation says that prophecies and tongues will pass away when the perfect comes, and continuationists argue, with real force, that the perfect is plainly the return of Christ, the moment we see face to face and know fully, not the closing of the canon, which the passage never mentions. So the burden of proof, they say, lies on the one claiming God turned something off, not on the one expecting him to keep doing what he never said he would stop. Beneath this argument is also something precious, a refusal to quench the Spirit the church is explicitly told never to quench, and behind it, also grief, because continuationists have watched a cold and mechanical Christianity that has functionally retired the living God and reduced him to a doctrine, and they have wanted the church to expect him to act. Sam Storms has made this case carefully, and Gordon Fee built a massive and serious study of the Spirit in Paul that presses it, and neither man is a thrill-seeker chasing sensation. They are exegetes refusing to silence a text. So there are the two cases, and I will not break the tie, and I want you to sit in the discomfort of that, because the discomfort is teaching you something. It is teaching you how tightly you want to hold a position that better Christians than you have disagreed about for centuries, and it is asking whether your certainty is serving the body of Christ or serving your need to be right. And here is the turn, and it is the thing that matters more than the verdict. In the middle of these very chapters, between the chapter that lists the gifts and the chapter that orders their use, Paul stops the argument cold and writes the greatest description of love ever set to paper. If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but have not love, I am a clanging gong. If I have prophetic powers and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, but have not love, I am nothing. Read where he placed that. Not in a letter about marriage or friendship. Right here, in the heart of the fight about gifts, as if to grab the Corinthians and us by the collar and say, you are about to make this the whole thing, and it is not the whole thing. The gifts are real. The gifts are not the point. A church that gets cessation exactly right and treats the continuationists down the road with contempt is a clanging gong. A church that gets continuation exactly right and despises the cautious cessationist is a clanging gong. The verdict of this session, then, is not a position. I am not handing you one. The verdict is a posture. Hold the disputed question with open hands, and hold the Spirit, and his church, and the love that outlasts every gift, with everything you have. Because when the perfect does come, however you read that phrase, the tongues will cease and the prophecies will pass and the knowledge we fought over will be swallowed up in seeing him face to face, and the only thing that will still be standing in that light is love.

scriptureStudy.note: Varieties of gifts but the same Spirit, and to each is given the manifestation for the common good. Whatever one believes about which gifts continue, the gifts are never for display or status but for building up the body, the common ground beneath the fight.

One and the same Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills. The Spirit chooses the distribution, which rebukes both the pride of the gifted and the envy of the ungifted, since no gift is earned and none is a measure of standing.

If I have all the gifts but have not love, I am nothing. Paul plants the love chapter in the middle of the gifts chapters deliberately, relativizing the whole dispute under the one thing that outlasts every gift.

Tongues will cease, prophecies will pass away, when the perfect comes. This is the central contested verse, the cessationist reading the perfect as the completed canon and the continuationist as the return of Christ, and the group should see why the phrase carries the weight it does.

Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. Paul commands both the pursuit of love and the desire for gifts in one breath, which the continuationist presses and which the cessationist must reckon with honestly.

Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone. The cessationist leans on the once-laid foundation, the unrepeatable apostolic role that certain gifts served to authenticate.

God bore witness by signs and wonders and gifts of the Holy Spirit. The text ties the signs to confirming the message, which the cessationist reads as their purpose now fulfilled and the continuationist reads as ongoing witness, a single verse both sides claim.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the actual history of this question, because the debate is older and more textured than the modern shouting suggests, and knowing the history lowers the temperature. The view that the most spectacular gifts had largely ceased after the apostolic age was held in various forms across much of church history, and B. B. Warfield gave it a famous and forceful statement in his work on miracles, arguing that the gifts were bound to the apostles and their authenticating function. Then the twentieth century brought the Pentecostal revivals and later the broader charismatic renewal across nearly every denomination, and a generation of careful scholars, among them Gordon Fee in his major study of the Spirit in the letters of Paul and Sam Storms and others, argued the continuationist case with exegetical seriousness rather than mere enthusiasm. A serious group should read at least one strong representative of each, ideally the side they instinctively oppose, and should weigh the genuinely difficult middle positions, the cautious or open-but-careful stance associated with figures who desire the gifts while insisting they never rival or add to Scripture. Weigh also the pastoral fruit and the pastoral danger on each side honestly, the deadness that can settle on a church that no longer expects God to act, and the chaos and manipulation that can overtake a church with no order and no test. The discipline this session requires, and the constitution of this whole platform requires, is the equal-weight steelman, the refusal to caricature, the ability to state the position you reject so faithfully that its best defenders would recognize themselves in your words. The aim is not to manufacture a false agreement but to produce a room that can disagree about a real and difficult question while remaining, unmistakably, one body, holding the same Lord, indwelt by the same Spirit, bound by the love Paul said would outlast every gift in the room.

memoryVerse.text: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

sessions.title: The Spirit and the Groaning
sessions.aim: To meet the Spirit at the place of our weakness, where we do not know how to pray and he intercedes in us with groanings too deep for words, and to receive his indwelling as the down payment of a whole new creation God has guaranteed.
sessions.summary: Paul says something staggering and easy to miss, that we do not know what to pray for as we ought, and that the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. The first question is what kind of God this is, who not only hears our prayers from above but prays inside us when we have run out of words. Bell brings the whole study here, because the Spirit who is fully God, who raises the dead and grows the fruit and gives the contested gifts, meets us finally not at the height of our strength but at the bottom of our weakness. Romans 8 sets the groaning in three layers. The creation groans, subjected to futility, waiting to be set free. We ourselves groan, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, waiting for the redemption of our bodies. And the Spirit groans within us, interceding when we cannot find the words. Bell takes the strong form of the objection, that this is just a religious name for inarticulate emotion, that calling your wordless ache an intercession of God is wishful labeling. He grants the ache is real and often wordless. But Paul says more, that the very inability to pray is the place the Spirit takes up the praying, that your groan is not the failure of prayer but the floor where God prays through you. Then the turn, and the end of the whole study. The Spirit is called the guarantee, the down payment, the firstfruits, the first installment of an inheritance God has bound himself to pay in full. The groaning is not despair. It is the labor pain of a creation being born again, and the Spirit in you is the proof that the birth is coming, God's own deposit, his pledge that he will finish what he started. The study does not resolve into ease. It leaves you groaning, with the Spirit groaning in you, toward a morning that is certain because God has put down the deposit himself.

keyScripture.why: Paul says the Spirit helps us in our weakness, that we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words, and the One who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, naming the Spirit as the One who prays inside us precisely when we cannot pray for ourselves.

discussion.q: Paul says we do not know what to pray for as we ought. Where have you sat down to pray and found you had no words, and what did you assume that wordlessness meant about you?
discussion.behind: Open on the common experience of not knowing how to pray. Most assume their wordlessness is a failure. The aim is to surface that assumption so the passage can overturn it, revealing the empty place not as the end of prayer but as where the Spirit takes it up.

discussion.q: The Spirit intercedes in us with groanings too deep for words. What changes when you hear that your wordless ache is not the failure of prayer but the floor where God begins to pray through you?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. We treat the groan as the breakdown of prayer. Paul treats it as the place the Spirit's prayer begins. The aim is to relocate the groan from evidence of weak faith to evidence of the indwelling God praying, which is enormous comfort to the worn out.

discussion.q: Bell takes the objection that calling our wordless ache an intercession of God is just wishful labeling. What is true in that caution, and how is Paul saying more than that?
