discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The caution against baptizing every feeling as God is healthy. The more is that Paul, by inspiration, names the Spirit as the actual one interceding, not merely our emotion renamed. Help the room hold reverent honesty without explaining the mystery away.

discussion.q: Romans 8 says the whole creation groans like a woman in labor, that the groaning is birth pain and not death rattle. How does naming your own groaning as labor rather than dying change how you carry it?
discussion.behind: Press on the image of labor. Birth pain is real agony but it points toward life, not death. The aim is for the room to feel that their groaning, and creation's, is the ache of something being born, which reframes suffering without minimizing it.

discussion.q: The Spirit is called the guarantee, the down payment on an inheritance God has promised to pay in full. As we close the whole study, what does it mean to you that God has put down a deposit of himself in you?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study on the indwelling Spirit as God's pledge. The aim is to gather all five sessions, the Spirit forgotten, the Spirit who births, who grows fruit, who gives gifts, and to land on him as God's own guarantee. Invite the room to name what the deposit assures them of. Go first.

objections.objection: Calling my wordless ache the intercession of the Holy Spirit is just wishful labeling. Sometimes I cannot pray because I am exhausted or empty or grieving, and dressing that up as God praying inside me is a comforting story I tell to feel less alone.
objections.response: Bell grants the caution, because it is healthy. Not every feeling is the voice of God, and the habit of baptizing every emotion as the Spirit has done real harm, and a wordless ache can indeed be only exhaustion or grief with nothing divine attached. So hold the honesty. But notice that Paul, writing by inspiration, says more than you are giving him room to say. He does not say your groaning feels meaningful. He says the Spirit himself intercedes for us, that the Spirit, a person, God, takes up the praying in the very place your words run out, and that the Father who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit and answers accordingly. This is not you relabeling your sadness. This is the claim that the God who lives in you prays through your weakness when you cannot pray at all, so that the emptiness you feared was the end of prayer is exactly where the truest praying is happening, under and beyond your words, by Someone who knows the will of God perfectly.

objections.objection: If the Spirit is the down payment and guarantees the inheritance, why is there still so much groaning, mine and the whole creation's? A guarantee that leaves everything still broken does not feel like much of a guarantee.
objections.response: Hold this gently, because it is the ache of everyone still waiting, and Paul does not pretend the waiting is light. He says the creation was subjected to futility, that it groans in the pains of childbirth, that we ourselves groan inwardly while we wait. The guarantee does not remove the groaning, and here is why that is not a contradiction. A down payment is precisely not the full payment, it is the binding pledge that the full payment is coming, money the giver would forfeit if he did not pay the rest. So the Spirit in you is not the absence of the brokenness, he is God's deposit inside the brokenness, his bound and costly promise that he will finish. And Paul gives the groaning a name, not death but birth, labor pains, which means the groaning is not the world running down toward nothing but a creation straining toward a life that is certainly coming, because the One who started the labor has put down a deposit of himself that he will not lose.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you have had no words to pray, did you carry it as your failure and your distance from God, when all along the Spirit may have been praying in you in a place deeper than language could reach?
sessions.practice: This week, on a day you cannot find words to pray, do not force them and do not give up. Instead sit quietly and say only this, Spirit, pray in me what I cannot say, and then stop talking and let the groan be the prayer. Do not fill the silence. Trust that the One who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, and that the wordless ache is being carried to the Father by Someone who knows exactly what to ask. Write down what it was like to let your weakness be the place of prayer rather than its end.
sessions.closingPrayer: Spirit of God, you meet us not at our strongest but at the bottom, where the words run out and the groaning begins, and you take up the praying we cannot do. We have carried our wordlessness as shame and our weakness as distance from God, when all along you were interceding in us with groanings too deep for words. Thank you that the very ache is being carried to the Father by you, who know his will perfectly. You are the down payment of a world being made new, God's own deposit in us, his pledge that the morning is coming. Hold us in the labor until the birth. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated my inability to pray as a failure, when Paul names it as the place the Spirit takes up the praying?
What in my life, or in the world, am I groaning over, and what changes if I name that groaning as labor pain toward a new creation rather than the slow dying of a broken one?
If the indwelling Spirit is God's down payment on an inheritance he has guaranteed, what does that deposit assure me of on the days nothing feels certain?
sessions.teaching: We end the study where the Christian life is actually lived, which is not at the summit of our strength but at the bottom of our weakness, because that is exactly where Paul places the Spirit in the eighth chapter of Romans. He says something so staggering we tend to read past it. We do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Stop on that. Paul, the apostle, the man who wrote half the New Testament, includes himself in the we who do not know how to pray. Not the immature believer, not the new convert, but all of us, the whole church, confessing that there are places we sit down to pray and have no idea what to ask, no words, only an ache. And here is the gospel buried in our incompetence. The God we have been studying for five sessions, the Spirit who is fully God, who raised us from spiritual death, who grows the slow fruit, who distributes the contested gifts, this same Spirit does not stand back and wait for us to compose ourselves. He intercedes. He takes up the praying we cannot do, inside us, with groanings too deep for words. What kind of God is this. Not only a God who hears prayer from his throne above, but a God who has come to live inside us and prays from there when we have run out of language. Romans 8 sets this groaning in three layers, and you have to see all three to feel the weight of it. First, the creation groans. Paul says the whole created order was subjected to futility, that it has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth right up to now, the whole world straining and aching under its brokenness, waiting to be set free. Second, we ourselves groan. We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, Paul says, groan inwardly as we wait for the redemption of our bodies, which means the groaning is not a sign you lack the Spirit, it is a sign you have him, the firstfruits, and so feel the gap between what is and what is coming. And third, underneath and within our groaning, the Spirit groans, interceding for us when we cannot find the words. Three groans, the creation's, ours, and God's own Spirit's, woven together in one labor. Now take the objection at full strength, because it is fair. Someone says, calling my wordless ache the intercession of the Holy Spirit is just wishful labeling. Sometimes I cannot pray because I am exhausted or grieving or empty, and dressing that emptiness up as God praying inside me is a comforting story I tell so I feel less alone. And grant the caution, because it is healthy. Not every feeling is the voice of God, and the church has done real damage baptizing every emotion as the Spirit, and a wordless ache can be only tiredness with nothing divine attached. Hold the honesty. But notice that Paul says more than you are giving him room to say. He does not say your groaning feels meaningful. He says the Spirit himself intercedes, that a person, God, takes up the praying precisely in the place your words give out, and that the Father who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit and answers what the Spirit asks. This is not you relabeling your sadness as holy. This is the claim that the God who lives in you is praying through your weakness when you cannot pray at all, so that the empty place you feared was the end of prayer turns out to be where the truest prayer in your life is happening, beneath your words, by Someone who knows the will of God perfectly and asks for exactly the right thing. And then comes the turn that ends the whole study, and it is the most hopeful word the Spirit's whole work contains. Throughout the New Testament the Spirit is given a particular name. He is called the guarantee of our inheritance, the down payment, the firstfruits, the first installment, the deposit. These are commercial words, on purpose. A down payment is money a buyer puts down that binds him to pay the rest, a pledge he would forfeit if he failed to complete the purchase, the part that guarantees the whole. And Paul says the Spirit in you is that, God's own deposit, the firstfruits of a harvest that is certainly coming, the binding pledge that he will finish the thing he started. Which means the groaning is not despair. Name it correctly. Paul does not call it a death rattle. He calls it the pains of childbirth, labor, and labor is agony that points not toward death but toward life, toward a child about to be born. The creation is not winding down toward nothing. It is groaning toward a new creation God has guaranteed, and the Spirit in you is the proof, the deposit, the down payment God himself has put down and will not lose. So this study does not end in resolution, and it should not, because we are not home yet, and a study that tied a bow on the Spirit would be lying about the age we live in. It ends in groaning, but it is the groaning of labor, not of dying, and you do not groan alone, because the God who is fully God, the forgotten God, the One who raised you and grows you and gives the gifts the church still argues over, is groaning inside you, praying what you cannot pray, the firstfruits of a morning that is coming as surely as God keeps his word, because he has put down the deposit himself. Carry the groaning out of this room. But carry it knowing whose groan joins yours, and toward what it is straining, and who has guaranteed the end. And here is the last word of the whole study, the thing all five sessions have been walking toward. The God we said we had forgotten, the one we reduced to a force and left a footnote, has not for one moment forgotten us. He has been here the entire time, in the room, in us, raising the dead, growing the fruit, distributing the gifts we argue over, and now praying in us when we cannot pray, the down payment God himself put down and will not lose. We were the ones who went absent. He never did. Go out groaning, then, but never again alone.

scriptureStudy.note: The Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what to pray for as we ought. Paul locates the Spirit's help precisely at the point of our incompetence, so weakness in prayer is not disqualification but the very place the Spirit goes to work.

He who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, who intercedes according to the will of God. The Spirit's wordless intercession is not vague feeling but prayer aligned perfectly with God's will, which is why it is the surest praying we ever do.

The whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth, and we ourselves groan inwardly. The groaning is named as labor, agony that points toward birth and not toward death, the creation and the believer alike straining toward redemption.

You received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry Abba, Father, the Spirit bearing witness that we are children of God. The same Spirit who groans in our weakness also assures us of our place in the family, the ground of all the praying.

You were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance. The Spirit is God's deposit, the binding pledge that the full inheritance is coming, his presence in us the proof that he will finish.

He has put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee. The Spirit is the down payment God has placed inside the believer, a commercial word for a binding first installment of what is promised in full.

For those who love God all things work together for good. Set right after the groaning and the Spirit's intercession, this promise is not a denial of the groaning but its outcome, the assurance under which the labor is endured.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the theme of the Spirit as firstfruits and guarantee across the whole sweep of redemption, because Paul's commercial language in Romans 8 and Ephesians 1 gathers up a vision of the future the modern church has often lost. The New Testament does not picture the Christian hope as souls escaping to a disembodied heaven but as the redemption of the body and the renewal of the whole creation, a new heavens and a new earth, and N. T. Wright has labored to recover this for a church that had quietly reduced its hope to going to heaven when we die. Read the groaning of Romans 8 against this larger hope and it comes into focus, the creation in labor is not waiting to be discarded but to be set free from its bondage to decay, and the believer's groaning body is not a prison to flee but a thing to be raised. A serious group should weigh how the Spirit functions as the link between this present age and the age to come, the firstfruits being the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees the rest, the down payment being the first installment that binds the giver to pay in full, so that the Spirit in us now is a genuine foretaste of the life of the world to come, not merely a promise about it but the first installment of it already given. Set this against the despair that watches the world groan and concludes it is simply running down, and against the false optimism that expects the groaning to end by human progress, and hold instead the Christian shape of hope, that the groaning is real and the renewal is certain because God has put down a deposit of himself. The discipline is to let this reframe both our prayer and our endurance, praying in the Spirit through our weakness and enduring the groaning as labor, because the One who began the work, who hovered over the first creation and raised Christ as the firstfruits of the new one, has guaranteed its completion with the gift of his own indwelling Spirit.

memoryVerse.text: Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to say yes to leading this, and the fact that you did matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only reach as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the material on the Spirit. It is asking honestly how well you yourself know the One the study is about. The aim of this series is narrow and it is weighty. It is to recover the Holy Spirit as fully God and fully personal and genuinely present, to refuse to leave him the forgotten member of the Trinity, and to do all of it without turning the room into a fight or a performance. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to make your group speak in tongues, and it is not to make them stop. It is not to settle the old debate about the gifts and send everyone home holding your position. It is not to manufacture an emotional experience so people feel they have met the Spirit. If anyone leaves this series more certain they are right and more contemptuous of the Christians who differ from them, the study failed, however orthodox it sounded. Keep that in front of you, because the single greatest danger you face as the leader of this particular study arrives in session four, where the question of the gifts can split a room down the middle in about ninety seconds. The whole point of that session, and the whole ethic of this platform, is the equal-weight steelman, the discipline of stating the position you disagree with so faithfully that its best defenders would say yes, that is exactly what we believe. You must model that. If you are a settled cessationist, you must be able to make the continuationist case so well that the continuationists in the room feel honored, and if you are a settled continuationist, you must do the same for the cessationist case. Do not break the tie for the group. Bell does not, and neither should you, because the divide here does not run between the faithful and the faithless. It runs through the middle of the godly, and a leader who turns it into a referendum will lose half the room and teach the other half contempt. The most important thing I can tell you about the heart of this study is that the Spirit is a person, not a force, and the entire series rises or falls on whether your people come to know him as someone they can grieve, welcome, address, and walk with, rather than a power they switch on for emotional moments. Watch your own language all the way through, because we have all been trained to call the Spirit an it without noticing, to say the Spirit fell or I felt the Spirit in ways we would never say of the Father. Catch yourself, and gently catch the room, not to scold but to retrain the grammar of how we think of God. Now keep the room safe, because two different kinds of wound will be sitting at your table. The first is the person who comes from a tradition that chased the Spirit hard, who has seen the gifts abused, who was manipulated by someone claiming a word from God, who is wary and maybe a little ashamed of where they came from. The second is the person from the opposite tradition, who has sat for decades in a church that functionally retired the Spirit, who has quietly hungered for more of God and been told that hunger was suspect. Both are wounded, in opposite directions, and both are in your room, and your job is to make it safe for both to be honest without either feeling attacked. Safety here does not mean avoiding the hard question. It means holding it in such a way that the cessationist and the continuationist can both speak, both be heard, and both leave still belonging to the same body. The moment someone in session four starts to argue to win rather than to understand, slow it down gently and turn the room back toward listening, and back toward the love chapter Paul planted in the middle of the fight on purpose. You will also meet a third kind of person, the one in session two who is not sure they have ever been born again at all, who has been religious for years and is quietly wondering, while everyone talks about the new birth, whether it ever happened to them. Handle this person with enormous tenderness. Do not press for a decision in the room or make a spectacle of anyone's uncertainty. The new birth is the Spirit's sovereign work and not something you can engineer with the right altar call, so your task is to keep pointing to Christ, to pray for the wind to blow, and to make yourself available afterward, quietly, to anyone who wants to talk. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own walk with the Spirit. You cannot lead people toward a God you have functionally forgotten. If you walk in as the expert dispensing doctrine about the third person of the Trinity while living, like most of us, as though the Father were distant and the Spirit absent, the room will feel the hollowness even if they cannot name it. Bell does not stand outside this. He confesses that he can preach the Trinity and then pray as though shouting at an empty sky, that he has lived whole weeks as though the God who raised Jesus were not at that moment dwelling in him. And he tells the harder story too, that he was an atheist, certain there was no God and no soul and no Spirit, and that what undid him was not an argument he lost but a presence he could not explain, so that he knows in a place beneath words that he did not author his own new birth. Bring your own honesty like that. If you have treated the Spirit as a stranger, say so. If your own conversion was a wind you did not summon, tell it. If you carry a settled position on the gifts and have to work to honor the other side, admit the work. The leader who says I am only beginning to know this person of God myself can lead the room without pretense, and pretense is the one thing that will kill this study. One more practical word before the charge. These five sessions move from doctrine toward the deepest weakness, and you should feel the arc. Session one recovers who the Spirit is. Session two takes us to the new birth we did not accomplish. Session three sits in the slow, sometimes discouraging work of being changed, and you must be ready for people who are disillusioned that they are not further along, and must normalize the slowness without excusing sin. Session four is the hard conversation, and you must protect the unity. And session five lands the whole study at the bottom, in the groaning, in the place where we cannot even find words to pray, and there you must be especially gentle, because some in the room are in exactly that wordless place right now. Do not rush past it. Let the silence in session five be long enough that people feel the Spirit may be praying in it. End every session in prayer, and in session five especially, trust the prayer to do what the discussion cannot. Resist the urge to resolve the study with a tidy summary of the Spirit, because the Spirit is God and will not fit in your summary, and the truest ending leaves the room groaning toward the new creation with the Spirit groaning in them. Here is your charge. You are not the expert on the Spirit in this room, and you are certainly not his manager. You are a fellow believer who is also only learning to know the person of God who has been living in you the whole time, pointing everyone, yourself first, toward him, and through him toward Christ, the way the Spirit himself always points. Lead like that. Recover the Spirit as a person your people can grieve and welcome and address. Hold the new birth as God's sovereign gift and not your altar-call technique. Be patient with slow change, in them and in yourself. Guard the unity through the hard session about gifts with everything you have, and refuse to let anyone leave it with contempt. And in the end, lead the room into its own weakness, into the groaning, and let them discover that they were never groaning alone. Go honestly. Go humbly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study going to push my group toward speaking in tongues, or away from it?
faq.a: Neither, and it works hard to do neither. The fourth session takes the question of whether gifts like tongues, prophecy, and healing continue today and refuses to settle it for the group, putting the continuationist case and the cessationist case at full and equal strength, because both are held by faithful, careful, Christ-loving believers and the divide runs through the middle of the godly rather than between the faithful and the faithless. The study deliberately does not break the tie. Its concern is not to win the old argument but to hold a room together across it, so that a group can disagree about which gifts continue while worshiping the same Spirit. If you came hoping the study would arm you for the fight, you will find instead a study that asks whether your certainty is serving the body of Christ or your need to be right.

faq.q: If I cannot describe the Holy Spirit very well, am I a bad Christian?
faq.a: No, and the first session opens by admitting that this is most of us. Ask a roomful of lifelong believers to describe the Father and the Son and they manage it, then ask them who the Spirit is and watch the pause. Francis Chan named him the forgotten God for a reason. The study treats this not as a private failure to scold but as a widespread loss to recover together, and it argues the reason we forget the Spirit is not that he is unimportant but that he is humble, because he does not point to himself, he points to Christ. We mistook his self-effacement for absence. So if the Spirit has been the vague one for you, you are exactly who this study is for, and the aim is to help you come to know him as the person of God he is, not to make you feel ignorant for not having known him sooner.

faq.q: The study says conversion is the Spirit's work. Does that mean my decision to follow Christ did not matter?
faq.a: No. The second session is careful to hold both truths at once. We really do decide, believe, repent, and come, and Scripture commands all of that and means it, and the one who comes is genuinely responsible for coming. But the study will not let the human decision swallow the divine act, because Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to decide harder, he tells him he must be born again, born of the Spirit, and a birth is the one thing you cannot perform on yourself. The mystery the church has always held is that the same event is fully the Spirit's work and truly your response, the wind that blows where it wills and the sail that genuinely catches it. The writer, an atheist made alive, found in his own experience a strong witness to the priority of grace, because he knows he did not begin the thing that saved him, and yet he truly came.

faq.q: Why does the writer keep bringing up his own atheism?
faq.a: Because it is the clearest evidence he has for what the second session claims, that the new birth is the Spirit's work and not the sinner's achievement. Bell was not a casual skeptic but a convinced atheist who had heard the arguments for God and had answers for them, and what finally changed him was not a syllogism he lost but a presence he had no category for, a wind that blew on a man who had not asked for it and could not have produced it. He brings it up because it guards the study from a lie we are all prone to, that the unconverted just need the right argument made, when in fact you do not argue a dead man into breathing. His story is not there to impress anyone. It is there to give every reader hope for the hardest skeptic they love, because too far gone is the only condition the Spirit has ever worked with.

faq.q: Why will the study not just tell me whether the miraculous gifts have ceased?
faq.a: Because the divide on that question does not run between faithful and faithless Christians, it runs through the middle of the godly, and a study that handed you a verdict would be misrepresenting the body of Christ. The cessationist case, carried by serious theologians like B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin, takes the sufficiency of Scripture and the unique foundational role of the apostles with deadly seriousness. The continuationist case, carried by serious theologians like Sam Storms and Gordon Fee, takes the absence of any biblical expiration date and Paul's command to desire the gifts just as seriously. The study puts both at full strength and then asks the harder question, whether you can hold the disputed point with open hands and the Spirit with everything you have, because Paul planted the greatest chapter on love in the middle of the gifts chapters on purpose, as if to say a church right about gifts and wrong about love is a clanging gong.

faq.q: I have been a Christian for years and I am not much more loving or patient than I was. Is something wrong with me?
faq.a: Not necessarily, and the third session is built to tell you the truth the church often hides, that sanctification is slow. Paul calls love and patience and the rest the fruit of the Spirit, and fruit grows at the speed of a tree, not the speed of a purchase, through seasons that can look like nothing is happening. The writer admits there are sins in him he assumed grace would have removed by now and has not, and names the two temptations the slowness produces, to give up and conclude the gospel does not work, or to fake it and hang plastic fruit on a branch that is not bearing. The study refuses both. The slowness is not proof of failure, it is the ordinary pace of real change, and the patience to keep walking while the fruit comes is itself one of the nine pieces of fruit the Spirit grows.

faq.q: Is the fruit of the Spirit just a nicer way of telling me to try harder?
faq.a: No, though the third session is careful to say that effort is real and Scripture does command it, since Paul says put sin to death and walk by the Spirit and no one drifts passively into holiness. The difference the word fruit makes is the difference between manufacturing a virtue by willpower and bearing it as the overflow of a connected life. Jesus gave the picture before Paul gave the list, the vine and the branches. A branch does the most active thing it can do, it refuses to detach, it stays joined to the vine, and out of that connection the fruit grows on its own. So your effort is not the effort of producing love by gritting your teeth, it is the effort of abiding, of keeping in step with the Spirit through prayer and the Word and obedience, while the fruit itself grows from the life you are joined to.

faq.q: What does it mean that the Spirit prays for me when I cannot pray?
faq.a: The fifth session takes this from Romans 8, where Paul says we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. It means your wordlessness in prayer, the times you sit down and have nothing to say, is not the failure of prayer but the floor where the Spirit takes up the praying. The God who lives in you prays through your weakness when you cannot pray at all, and the Father who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit and answers what the Spirit asks according to his will. The study is honest that not every feeling is the voice of God and warns against baptizing every emotion. But Paul says more than that our groaning feels meaningful. He says God himself is interceding in us, so the empty place we feared was the end of prayer turns out to be where the truest praying happens.

faq.q: The study keeps talking about groaning. Is it just telling me to expect suffering?
faq.a: It is telling you the truth about the age we live in, but it names the groaning carefully, and the name changes everything. Paul says the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth, that we ourselves groan inwardly, and that the Spirit groans within us, and the key word is childbirth, labor. Labor is real agony, but it points toward life, not death, toward a child about to be born. So the groaning is not the world running down toward nothing, it is a creation straining toward a new creation God has guaranteed. And the Spirit in you is called the down payment, the guarantee, the firstfruits, God's own deposit and binding pledge that he will finish what he started. The study does not promise the groaning ends now. It promises the One who began the labor has put down a deposit of himself that he will not lose.

faq.q: Does the study expect me to have some dramatic experience of the Spirit?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to engineer one. The leader primer warns the facilitator that the aim is not to manufacture an emotional experience so people feel they have met the Spirit, because the Spirit is God and not a feeling we summon. The study recovers the Spirit as a person to be known, grieved, welcomed, and walked with over a lifetime, not as a sensation to be chased on a given night. It honors the truth in the instinct that the Spirit is felt and fills and moves, while refusing the error that reduces him to the feelings, and it warns against a faith that becomes a hunt for sensations and calls every impulse divine guidance. What it asks of you is not an experience but a relationship, tested by the Word, with the God who already lives in you whether or not the room feels charged.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer and the leader instead of just teaching about the Spirit?
faq.a: Because the method is the message. Bell does not stand outside this as the expert dispensing doctrine about a God he has mastered. He admits he can preach the Trinity and then pray as though shouting at an empty sky, that he has lived whole weeks as though the indwelling God were not in the room, and that he came to faith from atheism by a wind he did not summon and cannot fully explain. The study asks every leader to bring the same honesty, because you cannot lead people toward a God you have functionally forgotten, and a leader who pretends to a settled mastery of the Spirit will ring hollow even where the doctrine is sound. A leader who says I am only beginning to know this person of God myself can lead the room without pretense, and pretense is the one thing that would kill a study about the living presence of God.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not this just Christians describing their feelings and calling it God?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it. It does not ask you to relabel your emotions as divine, in fact it warns Christians against doing exactly that, against baptizing every feeling as the Spirit. It grounds the personhood and deity of the Spirit in specific claims that can be examined, that he can be lied to and grieved and resisted, things you can only do to a someone, and it tells the story of a convinced atheist who was not argued into faith but changed by a presence he had no category for and did not want. You can weigh that story and find it insufficient, and the study does not pretend it is a proof. But it is not the soft thing you may expect, a believer dressing up a mood. It is a claim that there is a personal God who makes the dead alive, and you are invited to examine the claim, not to manufacture a feeling.

faq.q: How do I lead the session on spiritual gifts without my group falling into an argument?
faq.a: Carefully, and the leader primer treats this as the single greatest danger in the study. The discipline is the equal-weight steelman, stating the position you disagree with so faithfully that its best defenders would recognize themselves in your words. If you are a settled cessationist, you must make the continuationist case so well the continuationists feel honored, and if you are a settled continuationist, you must do the same for the cessationist. Do not break the tie for the group, because the divide runs through the middle of the godly and a leader who makes it a referendum will lose half the room and teach the other half contempt. When someone begins arguing to win rather than to understand, slow it down gently and turn the room back toward listening, and back toward the love Paul planted in the center of the gifts chapters. The goal is a room that can disagree about a real question while remaining, unmistakably, one body.

timeline.event: The Spirit of God hovers over the face of the waters at creation, present and active before there was anyone to feel him, so that the Spirit is no latecomer to the story of God but the breath of God at work from the first page.

Ezekiel prophesies that God will give his people a new heart and put a new spirit within them, removing the heart of stone, promising regeneration as God's own act centuries before Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born of the Spirit.

On the night before the cross Jesus promises the disciples another Helper, the Spirit of truth, to be with them forever and to dwell in them, naming the Spirit as a personal presence of the same kind as himself rather than a force sent from a distance.

After the resurrection and ascension the Spirit is poured out at Pentecost with the sound of a rushing wind and tongues of fire, and the church that had been waiting in an upper room is launched into the world by the presence of God.

Paul writes to the Corinthians on the spiritual gifts, naming their variety and their one Giver and one purpose, and plants in the middle of the discussion the greatest description of love ever written, relativizing every gift under the love that outlasts them.

Paul writes to the Romans that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding with groanings too deep for words, and that the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth, naming the Spirit as the One who prays in us and the firstfruits of a new creation.

A party arises denying the full deity of the Spirit, granting he is more than a creature but refusing to call him God, the controversy that forces the church to say clearly what it believes about the third person of the Trinity.

Basil of Caesarea writes his treatise on the Holy Spirit, arguing that the Spirit must be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, which is intelligible only if the Spirit is fully God.

The Council of Constantinople expands the creed to confess the Holy Spirit as the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, settling the deity of the Spirit for the church.

Martin Luther dies, having taught that the Spirit works faith through the Word and not apart from it, anchoring the experience of the Spirit to Scripture against both a dead formalism and an untethered enthusiasm.

The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles ignites the modern Pentecostal movement, reopening across the worldwide church the question of whether the miraculous gifts continue, a question that will shape much of the next century of debate.

B. B. Warfield publishes his influential argument that the miraculous gifts were bound to the apostles and their authenticating work and ceased with the apostolic age, giving the modern cessationist position its most forceful statement.

Gordon Fee publishes his major study of the Spirit in the letters of Paul, a serious exegetical case for the continuing presence and gifting of the Spirit, marking the maturing of careful continuationist scholarship.
Francis Chan publishes Forgotten God, calling the church to reckon with how thoroughly it has neglected the Holy Spirit, the title that names the wound this whole study sets out to address.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for being willing to spend five weeks on the member of the Trinity most of us know the least. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can admit here that you have never really known the Holy Spirit, that he has been the vague one for you, and no one is going to make you feel foolish for it, because that is most of us. Second, this study is not going to push you toward speaking in tongues or away from it, and when we reach the session on the gifts, we are going to put both sides at their strongest and refuse to settle the fight, because faithful Christians who love the same Lord land on opposite sides of it. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. He came to faith from atheism by a presence he could not explain, and he admits he can know the doctrine and still live as though God were far off. We are not experts standing over the Spirit. We are people only beginning to know the God who has been living in us the whole time. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says about the Spirit. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the ordinary week, into the prayers we do not know how to pray and the change that comes slower than we want and the God we keep forgetting is already in the room, because that is where this either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it does not tie up neatly, because the Spirit is God and will not fit inside a tidy summary, and the truest thing we can do is keep walking with him rather than pretend we have him figured out. Take this toward the Spirit himself this week rather than just thinking about him. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if tonight stirred a hunger to know this person of God you have long forgotten, follow it, because he has been waiting, with great patience, to be known. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and about the gifts session to come, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Begin retraining the room to speak of the Spirit as a person.
Week 2: Session 1, The Spirit We Ignore, full discussion and practice on the personhood and deity of the Spirit.
Week 3: Session 2, Born of the Spirit, with extended time on the new birth as resurrection and the writer's own conversion from atheism.
Week 4: Session 3, The Fruit and the Walk, part one through the difference between fruit and performance and the two errors about sanctification.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the vine and the branches, abiding and walking, and honest time on the slowness of real change.
Week 6: Session 4, Gifts and the Contested Question, with extended time to build both the cessationist and continuationist cases at full strength.
Week 7: Session 5, The Spirit and the Groaning, the Spirit who intercedes in our weakness and the Spirit as the down payment of the new creation.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person now wants to bring to the Spirit they had forgotten, with space for anyone unsure of the new birth to talk.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, who the Spirit is and the new birth he alone accomplishes.
Week 2: Session 3, The Fruit and the Walk, with extended time on abiding and the slowness of sanctification.
Week 3: Session 4, Gifts and the Contested Question, both cases built at full strength and the unity of the body guarded.
Week 4: Session 5, The Spirit and the Groaning, plus a short integration close on the Spirit as God's down payment in us.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, The Spirit We Ignore.
Week 2: Session 2, Born of the Spirit.
Week 3: Session 3, The Fruit and the Walk.
Week 4: Session 4, Gifts and the Contested Question.
Week 5: Session 5, The Spirit and the Groaning.

bibliography.title: Forgotten God: Reversing Our Tragic Neglect of the Holy Spirit
bibliography.author: Francis Chan
bibliography.note: The book that names the wound this whole study addresses, calling the church to reckon with how thoroughly it has neglected the Spirit. The pastoral spine of session 1.

bibliography.title: Keep in Step with the Spirit: Finding Fullness in Our Walk with God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: Takes its title from Galatians 5 and argues for a sanctification that is neither gritted self-effort nor passive let go and let God, but an active dependence. Anchors session 3.

bibliography.title: God's Empowering Presence: The Holy Spirit in the Letters of Paul
bibliography.author: Gordon Fee
bibliography.note: A major exegetical study of the Spirit in Paul that presses the continuationist case with seriousness rather than enthusiasm. A primary witness for the continuationist side in session 4. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Cessation of the Charismata, and broader writing on the miraculous gifts
bibliography.author: B. B. Warfield
bibliography.note: The most forceful modern statement of the cessationist case, arguing the miraculous gifts were bound to the apostles and their authenticating work. A primary witness for the cessationist side in session 4. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: Perspectives on Pentecost, and writing on the gifts and the apostolic foundation
bibliography.author: Richard Gaffin
bibliography.note: A careful Reformed presentation of the cessationist case centered on the unique, unrepeatable foundational role of the apostles. Supports the cessationist steelman in session 4. Leader to confirm the specifics before stating them as the study's position.

bibliography.title: Practicing the Power, and broader writing for the continuationist position
bibliography.author: Sam Storms
bibliography.note: A careful continuationist who argues the New Testament names no expiration date for the gifts and that Paul commands believers to desire them. Supports the continuationist steelman in session 4. Leader to confirm before attributing claims to Bell.

bibliography.title: On the Holy Spirit
bibliography.author: Basil of Caesarea
bibliography.note: The fourth-century treatise arguing that the Spirit must be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son, foundational to the church's confession of the Spirit's deity. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: Surprised by the Spirit, and broader writing on new creation and the Spirit
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Recovers the Christian hope as the renewal of creation and the redemption of the body rather than escape to a disembodied heaven, framing the Spirit as the firstfruits of that hope. Supports session 5. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as Bell's own argument.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the tenderness of Christ toward the weary, a useful companion to the Spirit who meets us at the bottom of our weakness in session 5, where the Spirit prays what we cannot.

bibliography.title: The Holy Spirit
bibliography.author: Sinclair Ferguson
bibliography.note: A careful theological treatment of the person and work of the Spirit across the whole sweep of Scripture, balanced and pastoral. Useful across all five sessions. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as the study's position.

bibliography.title: The Mystery of the Holy Spirit
bibliography.author: R. C. Sproul
bibliography.note: An accessible introduction to the deity and personhood of the Spirit and his work in regeneration and sanctification. Supports sessions 1 through 3. Offered as a balancing Reformed voice.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The account of a mind that resisted God and was finally drawn by grace it did not summon, a companion to the writer's own conversion from unbelief in session 2. Background for the priority of grace in the new birth.

furtherReading: Forgotten God, Francis Chan, for readers who want to sit longer with the church's neglect of the Spirit and the call to know him as a person, which anchors session 1.

Keep in Step with the Spirit, J. I. Packer, for those who want a fuller treatment of sanctification that holds effort and grace together against both the treadmill and the hammock, supporting session 3.

God's Empowering Presence, Gordon Fee, for readers who want the continuationist case made with full exegetical seriousness, read alongside a strong cessationist for session 4, leader to confirm specific claims.
Perspectives on Pentecost, Richard Gaffin, for readers who want the cessationist case made carefully from the apostolic foundation, read alongside a strong continuationist for session 4.

The Holy Spirit, Sinclair Ferguson, for those who want a balanced, full study of the person and work of the Spirit across the whole of Scripture, read alongside the study's recovery of the forgotten God.

glossary.definition: The third person of the one God, of one being with the Father and the Son, fully divine and fully personal, who can be grieved, lied to, and resisted, and who has come to live inside the people of God. Not a force or an influence but God himself, present and indwelling.

The new birth, the Spirit's act of making the spiritually dead alive, named by Jesus as being born again or born of the Spirit. Not the improvement of the old self but a resurrection, a thing done to us by God and not accomplished by us.

The Spirit's living presence inside the believer, the with you and in you that Jesus promised, so that the Christian is not visited by God from a distance but inhabited by him, the body of the believer a temple of the Holy Spirit.

The cluster of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control that the Spirit grows in the believer, named as fruit rather than works to mark it as the overflow of a connected life rather than the product of willpower.

The slow, lifelong process by which the Spirit makes the believer actually holy, growing the fruit at the speed of a tree rather than a purchase, held between the errors of gritted self-effort and passive waiting, lived as abiding in the Vine and keeping in step with the Spirit.

The varieties of grace the Spirit distributes among believers as he wills, for the common good and the building up of the body, never for status or display, the subject of the long-disputed question of which gifts continue today.

The position that certain miraculous gifts, such as tongues, prophecy, and healing, served to authenticate the apostles and the giving of Scripture and ceased when the apostolic foundation was laid and the canon completed. Held by serious believers for serious reasons, and put at full strength in session 4.

The position that the New Testament names no expiration date for the gifts before Christ returns, that Paul commands believers to desire them, and that they continue in the church today. Held by serious believers for serious reasons, and put at full strength in session 4.

The discipline this study requires on contested questions, the practice of stating the position you disagree with so faithfully that its best defenders would recognize themselves in your words, refusing to caricature the other side in order to win.

The Spirit's praying within the believer, taking up the praying we cannot do, interceding with groanings too deep for words at the very point where our own words run out, according to the will of God.

The ache of the creation, the believer, and the Spirit named in Romans 8, called the pains of childbirth, agony that points toward birth and not death, the labor of a creation straining toward the redemption God has guaranteed.

The Spirit named as the down payment, deposit, and firstfruits of the believer's inheritance, a commercial term for the binding first installment that pledges the giver to pay in full, so that the Spirit in us is God's own deposit guaranteeing he will finish what he started.

The historic confession, settled at Constantinople, that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, eternally and not as a creature, the language by which the church guarded the full deity of the Spirit within the one God.
